content: A continuous wave (CW) is an electromagnetic wave characterized by a constant amplitude and frequency, and in mathematical terms, it is considered to have an infinite duration. Historically, the term continuous wave also referred to an early method of radio transmission in which a carrier wave was switched on and off. The information in this system was encoded in the varying durations of the on and off periods of the signal. In the context of radio transmission, CW waves are also referred to as undamped waves, distinguishing them from the earlier damped wave transmission methods. Early radio transmitters utilized spark gaps to generate radio-frequency oscillations in the transmitting antenna. The signals produced by these spark-gap transmitters exhibited a rapidly damped amplitude during each pulse of radiated energy. With the advent of alternators and later electronic oscillators, the signal strength remained constant during each code element, leading to the description of this technique as continuous waves. An unmodulated carrier wave has no bandwidth and conveys no information; however, the act of keying the carrier on and off introduces a finite bandwidth related to the transmission rate. Technically, a keyed carrier may be referred to as interrupted continuous wave (ICW), but the necessity of keying is generally understood in this context. In the early days of radio, transmitters were not capable of handling the complexity of actual audio signals, making CW the only viable form of communication. Even after the development of voice transmission, CW remained a practical method of radio communication for many years due to the simplicity of the required transmitters. The low bandwidth of the CW code signal, partly due to its low information transmission rate, allowed for the use of highly selective filters in receivers. These filters effectively blocked much of the atmospheric noise that would otherwise degrade the intelligibility of the signal. Continuous-wave radio was often referred to as radiotelegraphy because, like the telegraph, it operated using a simple switch to transmit Morse code. However, instead of controlling electricity in a cross-country wire, the switch controlled the power sent to a radio transmitter. This mode of communication is still commonly used by amateur radio operators today. A continuous-wave radar system operates by transmitting a continuous wave from one antenna while a second antenna receives the reflected radio energy. In amateur radio, the terms CW and Morse code are often used interchangeably, despite the technical distinctions between the two. Morse code can be transmitted using direct current in wires, sound, or light, among other methods. In Morse code transmission, if the carrier wave is turned on or off too quickly, the resulting bandwidth will be large. Conversely, if the carrier is turned on and off more gradually, the bandwidth will be smaller. The issue of excessive bandwidth caused by a Morse transmitter that switches on and off too rapidly is known as key clicks. Certain types of power amplifiers used in transmitters can exacerbate the problematic effects of key clicks. In the field of laser physics and engineering, the term continuous wave (CW) refers to a laser that produces a continuous output beam, sometimes described as free-running. This is in contrast to Q-switched, gain-switched, or mode-locked lasers, which produce pulses of light.
